The Arabs conquered Khurasan by treaty in 30 AH/650 CE, during the caliphate of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān. But revolts and other forms of resistance to Arab rule continued through almost the entire Umayyad period, and then returned under the Abbasids in many new forms, including intellectual and ideological ones. Under al-Manṣūr, the people of Khurasan revolted against him in 136 AH/753 CE. See Murūj al-Dhahab, vol. 2, p. 237.↩︎
Khurasan was one of the main centers of the Alids and later of Abbasid propaganda against the Umayyads. It remained an important center of Shiʿism throughout Islamic history.↩︎

During the caliphate of the Umayyad Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik (105–125 AH/723–742 CE), for example, the people of Khurasan took an active part in the revolt of Zayd ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in 121 AH/738 CE. See Ibn al-Ṭiqṭaqā, al-Fakhrī fī al-Ādāb al-Sulṭāniyya, p. 113. Historians have usually explained revolts like this purely in sectarian terms—as expressions of Shiʿism—while neglecting their social motives. Yet for many participants, the main motives were less sectarian than they were forms of resistance to social or political domination. This applies very clearly to the people of Khurasan at the time.↩︎

Sufi sources tell us that Ibrāhīm ibn Adham lived in Basra, Alexandria, and Mecca and later in Syria. See Ṭabaqāt al-Ṣūfiyya, p. 30. They say that al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ went to Kufa and lived there; see Jāmī, Nafaḥāt al-Uns, p. 38. He died in 187 AH/803 CE; see Ibn al-Jawzī, Ṣifat al-Ṣafwa, vol. 2, p. 134. Ibn al-Mubārak left Khurasan for Kufa; see ibid., vol. 4, p. 109. The sources disagree over the journeys, beliefs, and fate of Shaqīq al-Balkhī. The author of al-Kawākib al-Durriyya (vol. 1, p. 121) says that he once set out accompanied by 300 poor worshippers and ascetics, and that he met the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn and admonished him. Nafaḥāt al-Uns (p. 15) presents him as Sunni, while Rawḍāt al-Jannāt (p. 328) presents him as a Jaʿfari and says that he was martyred in Transoxiana on a charge of rafḍ, or Shiʿism. Nafaḥāt al-Uns (p. 50) says that he was martyred in the province of Khuttal, and so on.↩︎

Rābiʿa al-ʿAdawiyya was born into a very poor family in Basra and was connected to Banū ʿAdwa through clientage rather than descent. When she was still young, her father died and a famine struck Basra. She and her three sisters became separated and wandered without direction. A cruel man captured her and sold her for six dirhams to a man who worked her very hard. One day, as she was walking, she noticed a man looking at her with bad intentions and ran away. On the road she threw herself onto the ground and prayed to God. She then heard a voice say: “Do not grieve. On the Day of Judgment, those closest to God in heaven will look toward you and envy what you will become.” After hearing this, she returned to her “master’s” house, began fasting, continued serving him, and spent the whole night in prayer. See Badawī, Shahīdat al-ʿIshq al-Ilāhī, Cairo, 1962, 2nd ed., pp. 8, 12. Even this summary still contains a legendary element at the end of the story.↩︎

This began when Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān founded the Umayyad state in 40 AH/660 CE. Muʿāwiya made its political system an absolute monarchy and then made the monarchy hereditary within a dynasty. This political system continued through the later periods of the Islamic caliphate. Muʿāwiya seems to have chosen this system with a conscious understanding of what kingship meant in the civilization of the time, as shown by the fact that he himself took pride in being “the first king” in Arab-Islamic history. See Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, al-Istīʿāb, vol. 1, p. 254.↩︎

One Western scholar of Arab civilization noticed, in his own way, this relationship between philosophy and Islamic Sufism. He wrote that “mysticism among Muslims also clearly shows its close relationship and kinship with rational thought, a relationship that can be demonstrated throughout world history, because mysticism too is a science with principles of its own, and its opposite is not theoretical scientific knowledge...” See Adam Mez, Die Renaissance des Islams, vol. 2, p. 14, 3rd Arabic ed. Mez means here that Sufism is itself a kind of “theoretical scientific knowledge,” rather than its opposite. This is the basis on which we study Sufism as part of the history of Arab-Islamic philosophy.↩︎

Abū Saʿīd Aḥmad ibn Saʿīd al-Kharrāz (d. 277 AH/890 CE), one of the major Sufis of the third Islamic century, says: “...Knowledge of the Truth [God] is knowledge of His oneness.” al-Sarrāj al-Ṭūsī, al-Lumaʿ, p. 56.↩︎

An example is Adam Mez’s claim that from the third Islamic century onward Muslims began to feel new religious needs, and that “the old religions that had always remained hidden behind an outward veil, especially Christianity—that is, the body of late Greek philosophy in its Christianized schools and forms,” by which he means Neoplatonism, “quickly came forward to meet these needs. The movement that changed the form of Islam during the third and fourth centuries was, taken as a whole, nothing but the result of Christian intellectual currents entering the religion of Muḥammad.” Mez then says, in the same context, that the idea of knowing God “as the highest religious ideal belongs to the ancient Gnostic doctrine. Among free thinkers it appeared as rationalism or scientific theology, and among others as mysticism.” On Mez’s view, then, the Sufi theory of knowledge comes entirely from two external sources: Christianity in its Neoplatonic form, and ancient Eastern Gnosticism. Similar views can be found among other Arab and Orientalist scholars. See, for example, Nicholson, Studies in Islamic Mysticism, Arabic trans. Abū al-ʿAlā ʿAfīfī, p. 14 ff.; and Ḥannā al-Fākhūrī and Khalīl al-Jurr, Tārīkh al-Falsafa al-ʿArabiyya, Beirut, vol. 1, p. 301, on the Sufi Dhū al-Nūn al-Miṣrī.↩︎

al-Risāla al-Qushayriyya says: “Abū al-Fayḍ Dhū al-Nūn al-Miṣrī, whose name was Thawbān ibn Ibrāhīm, and whose father was Nubian, from the land of Nubia.” Nicholson calls him “the true founder of Sufism” (Studies in Islamic Mysticism, Arabic trans. Abū al-ʿAlā ʿAfīfī, Cairo, 1947, p. 7). Philip Hitti calls him “the founder of Sufi doctrine” (History of the Arabs, extended ed., vol. 2, p. 524, Beirut, 1950). Albert Naṣrī Nādir argues that Dhū al-Nūn al-Miṣrī was “the first to make philosophy a part of Sufism” (al-Taṣawwuf al-Islāmī, Beirut, 1960, p. 42). We may not regard such exact claims as scientifically sound, since intellectual phenomena, like other phenomena, cannot be dated as though they suddenly came into existence through one person without earlier roots or preparation. Even so, these claims remain significant because they show the historical importance of Dhū al-Nūn’s thought within philosophical Sufism.↩︎

We took this passage from Kāmil Muṣṭafā al-Shaybī, al-Ṣila bayna al-Taṣawwuf wa-l-Tashayyuʿ, p. 363, translated from Farīd al-Dīn ʿAṭṭār’s Persian Tadhkirat al-Awliyāʾ, vol. 1, p. 108. Another translation of the same passage from the same source appears at vol. 1, p. 127, and reads: “True knowledge of God is not knowledge of His oneness, which all believers possess. Nor is it the demonstrative and speculative knowledge of the philosophers, theologians, and men of eloquence. Rather, it is knowledge of the qualities of oneness, a knowledge belonging especially to the saints, because they are the ones who behold God with their hearts, and He reveals to them what He does not reveal to His other servants.” See Albert Nādir, al-Taṣawwuf al-Islāmī, Beirut, 1960, p. 20. The clear difference between the two translations does not affect Dhū al-Nūn’s picture of Sufi knowledge, the knowledge of the saints. But it does affect his attitude toward the other two kinds of knowledge. In the first translation, he seems to recognize the knowledge of believers and the rational knowledge of philosophers alongside the knowledge of the saints, or Sufis. In the second, he appears to reject the other two and recognize only Sufi knowledge.↩︎

Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī was among the earliest Muslims and among the earliest Islamic ascetics. He supported ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and opposed ʿUthmān and Muʿāwiya. In 30 AH, Muʿāwiya expelled him from Syria to Medina, and Caliph ʿUthmān later exiled him to the village of al-Rabadha near Medina because of his strong opposition to the caliph’s policies and to the enrichment of the Umayyads at the expense of the poor masses.↩︎
